AI.motivation: Existing benchmarks for LLM mathematical capabilities rely on static, hand-curated contest or textbook problems, which don't accurately reflect research-level mathematics. There's a need for benchmarks that directly evaluate models on actual mathematical research.
AI.method: Developed an automatic pipeline that extracts lemmas from arXiv papers and rewrites them into self-contained statements by making all assumptions and required definitions explicit. This creates an updatable benchmark that can be regularly refreshed with new research problems.
AI.result: Current state-of-the-art LLMs achieve approximately 10-15% accuracy (pass@1) in theorem proving on this benchmark, indicating a significant performance gap compared to human-level proving capabilities in research contexts.
AI.conclusion: The proposed benchmark provides a more realistic assessment of LLM capabilities on research mathematics, reveals substantial room for improvement in theorem proving, and enables ongoing evaluation without compromising future assessments through its updatable design.

title: ArgLLM-App: An Interactive System for Argumentative Reasoning with Large Language Models
summary: Argumentative LLMs (ArgLLMs) are an existing approach leveraging Large Language Models (LLMs) and computational argumentation for decision-making, with the aim of making the resulting decisions faithfully explainable to and contestable by humans. Here we propose a web-based system implementing ArgLLM-empowered agents for binary tasks. ArgLLM-App supports visualisation of the produced explanations and interaction with human users, allowing them to identify and contest any mistakes in the system's reasoning. It is highly modular and enables drawing information from trusted external sources. ArgLLM-App is publicly available at https://argllm.app, with a video demonstration at https://youtu.be/vzwlGOr0sPM.

AI.tldr: ArgLLM-App is a web-based system implementing argumentative LLM agents for binary decision-making tasks, featuring visualization of explanations and human interaction for contesting reasoning errors.
AI.motivation: To create a practical system that makes LLM-based decisions explainable and contestable by humans, addressing the need for transparency and accountability in AI decision-making.
AI.method: Developed a modular web-based system implementing ArgLLM-empowered agents for binary tasks, supporting visualization of explanations, human interaction for contesting mistakes, and integration with trusted external sources.
AI.result: Created ArgLLM-App, a publicly available system at https://argllm.app with video demonstration, enabling users to visualize AI reasoning and contest any identified mistakes in the system's decision-making process.
AI.conclusion: ArgLLM-App provides a practical implementation of argumentative LLMs for transparent decision-making, offering both explanation visualization and human contestation capabilities to enhance trust and accountability in AI systems.

title: Task-Centric Acceleration of Small-Language Models
summary: Small language models (SLMs) have emerged as efficient alternatives to large language models for task-specific applications. However, they are often employed in high-volume, low-latency settings, where efficiency is crucial. We propose TASC, Task-Adaptive Sequence Compression, a framework for SLM acceleration comprising two use-cases: When performing SLM fine-tuning, we propose TASC-ft, which iteratively enriches the tokenizer vocabulary with high-frequency output n-grams and then fine-tunes the model to utilize the expanded vocabulary. Next, we propose an inference-time method, termed TASC-spec. TASC-spec is a lightweight, training-free speculative decoding method that constructs an n-gram draft model from the task's output corpus, mixing task and context n-gram information.TASC-spec avoids any additional training, while bypassing draft-target vocabulary alignment constraints. We demonstrate the effectiveness of both methods across multiple low output-variability generation tasks. Our methods show consistent improvements in inference efficiency while maintaining task performance.

AI.tldr: TASC framework accelerates small language models via task-adaptive sequence compression with two methods: TASC-ft for fine-tuning with enriched vocabulary, and TASC-spec for training-free speculative decoding using n-gram drafts.
AI.motivation: Small language models are deployed in high-volume, low-latency settings where efficiency is crucial, but they lack the acceleration techniques available to larger models. There's a need for task-specific optimization methods that can improve inference efficiency while maintaining performance.
AI.method: TASC framework includes two approaches: 1) TASC-ft: During fine-tuning, iteratively enriches tokenizer vocabulary with high-frequency output n-grams, then fine-tunes model to use expanded vocabulary. 2) TASC-spec: Inference-time speculative decoding method that constructs lightweight n-gram draft model from task's output corpus, mixing task and context n-gram information without additional training.
AI.result: The methods demonstrate consistent improvements in inference efficiency across multiple low output-variability generation tasks while maintaining task performance. TASC-spec avoids additional training and bypasses draft-target vocabulary alignment constraints.
AI.conclusion: TASC provides effective task-adaptive sequence compression for SLM acceleration through complementary fine-tuning and inference-time methods, offering practical efficiency gains for high-volume, low-latency applications without compromising task performance.

title: Uncertainty Quantification for Multimodal Large Language Models with Incoherence-adjusted Semantic Volume
comment: Earlier versions presented at ICLR 2025 QUESTION workshop and ICML 2025 R2-FM workshop
summary: Despite their capabilities, Multimodal Large Language Models (MLLMs) may produce plausible but erroneous outputs, hindering reliable deployment. Accurate uncertainty metrics could enable escalation of unreliable queries to human experts or larger models for improved performance. However, existing uncertainty metrics have practical constraints, such as being designed only for specific modalities, reliant on external tools, or computationally expensive. We introduce UMPIRE, a training-free uncertainty quantification framework for MLLMs that works efficiently across various input and output modalities without external tools, relying only on the models' own internal modality features. UMPIRE computes the incoherence-adjusted semantic volume of sampled MLLM responses for a given task instance, effectively capturing both the global semantic diversity of samples and the local incoherence of responses based on internal model confidence. We propose uncertainty desiderata for MLLMs and provide theoretical analysis motivating UMPIRE's design. Extensive experiments show that UMPIRE consistently outperforms baseline metrics in error detection and uncertainty calibration across image, audio, and video-text benchmarks, including adversarial and out-of-distribution settings. We also demonstrate UMPIRE's generalization to non-text output tasks, including image and audio generation.

AI.tldr: UMPIRE is a training-free uncertainty quantification framework for Multimodal Large Language Models that computes incoherence-adjusted semantic volume of sampled responses, outperforming existing methods across various modalities without external tools.
AI.motivation: MLLMs produce plausible but erroneous outputs that hinder reliable deployment. Existing uncertainty metrics have practical constraints: modality-specific designs, reliance on external tools, or computational expense. There's a need for efficient, generalizable uncertainty quantification across modalities.
AI.method: UMPIRE computes incoherence-adjusted semantic volume of sampled MLLM responses using only internal modality features. It captures both global semantic diversity of samples and local incoherence based on internal model confidence, without training or external tools.
AI.result: UMPIRE consistently outperforms baseline metrics in error detection and uncertainty calibration across image, audio, and video-text benchmarks, including adversarial and out-of-distribution settings. It also generalizes to non-text output tasks like image and audio generation.
AI.conclusion: UMPIRE provides an effective, training-free uncertainty quantification framework for MLLMs that works efficiently across various input and output modalities without external tools, addressing practical constraints of existing methods and enabling more reliable deployment.

title: MT-PingEval: Evaluating Multi-Turn Collaboration with Private Information Games
summary: We present a scalable methodology for evaluating language models in multi-turn interactions, using a suite of collaborative games that require effective communication about private information. This enables an interactive scaling analysis, in which a fixed token budget is divided over a variable number of turns. We find that in many cases, language models are unable to use interactive collaboration to improve over the non-interactive baseline scenario in which one agent attempts to summarize its information and the other agent immediately acts -- despite substantial headroom. This suggests that state-of-the-art models still suffer from significant weaknesses in planning and executing multi-turn collaborative conversations. We analyze the linguistic features of these dialogues, assessing the roles of sycophancy, information density, and discourse coherence. While there is no single linguistic explanation for the collaborative weaknesses of contemporary language models, we note that humans achieve comparable task success at superior token efficiency by producing dialogues that are more coherent than those produced by most language models. The proactive management of private information is a defining feature of real-world communication, and we hope that MT-PingEval will drive further work towards improving this capability.

AI.tldr: Language models struggle with multi-turn collaborative conversations despite having substantial headroom for improvement, performing worse than non-interactive baselines in games requiring communication about private information.
AI.motivation: To evaluate language models' capabilities in multi-turn collaborative interactions, particularly their ability to effectively communicate about private information - a defining feature of real-world communication that current models may lack.
AI.method: Developed MT-PingEval, a scalable evaluation methodology using collaborative games requiring private information communication. Used interactive scaling analysis where fixed token budget is divided over variable turns, comparing interactive vs. non-interactive baselines. Analyzed linguistic features including sycophancy, information density, and discourse coherence.
AI.result: Language models fail to leverage interactive collaboration to outperform non-interactive baselines (where one agent summarizes information and the other acts immediately), despite substantial headroom. Humans achieve comparable task success with superior token efficiency through more coherent dialogues. No single linguistic factor explains models' collaborative weaknesses.
AI.conclusion: State-of-the-art language models still have significant weaknesses in planning and executing multi-turn collaborative conversations. The MT-PingEval framework provides a tool for driving improvements in models' ability to proactively manage private information during communication.

title: A Minimal Agent for Automated Theorem Proving
summary: We propose a minimal agentic baseline that enables systematic comparison across different AI-based theorem prover architectures. This design implements the core features shared among state-of-the-art systems: iterative proof refinement, library search and context management. We evaluate our baseline using qualitatively different benchmarks and compare various popular models and design choices, and demonstrate competitive performance compared to state-of-the-art approaches, while using a significantly simpler architecture. Our results demonstrate consistent advantages of an iterative approach over multiple single-shot generations, especially in terms of sample efficiency and cost effectiveness. The implementation is released open-source as a candidate reference for future research and as an accessible prover for the community.

AI.tldr: A minimal agentic baseline for AI theorem provers that enables systematic comparison across architectures, featuring iterative proof refinement, library search, and context management, achieving competitive performance with simpler design.
AI.motivation: To establish a standardized baseline for comparing different AI-based theorem prover architectures, addressing the need for systematic evaluation across diverse approaches and enabling clearer understanding of design choices.
AI.method: Develops a minimal agentic baseline implementing core features shared by state-of-the-art systems: iterative proof refinement, library search, and context management. Evaluates using qualitatively different benchmarks and compares various popular models and design choices.
AI.result: Demonstrates competitive performance compared to state-of-the-art approaches while using significantly simpler architecture. Shows consistent advantages of iterative approach over multiple single-shot generations, particularly in sample efficiency and cost effectiveness.
AI.conclusion: The minimal baseline provides a valuable reference for future research and an accessible prover for the community, highlighting the effectiveness of iterative approaches and the importance of systematic architectural comparisons in AI theorem proving.

title: Controllable Reasoning Models Are Private Thinkers
summary: AI agents powered by reasoning models require access to sensitive user data. However, their reasoning traces are difficult to control, which can result in the unintended leakage of private information to external parties. We propose training models to follow instructions not only in the final answer, but also in reasoning traces, potentially under different constraints. We hypothesize that improving their instruction following abilities in the reasoning traces can improve their privacy-preservation skills. To demonstrate this, we fine-tune models on a new instruction-following dataset with explicit restrictions on reasoning traces. We further introduce a generation strategy that decouples reasoning and answer generation using separate LoRA adapters. We evaluate our approach on six models from two model families, ranging from 1.7B to 14B parameters, across two instruction-following benchmarks and two privacy benchmarks. Our method yields substantial improvements, achieving gains of up to 20.9 points in instruction-following performance and up to 51.9 percentage points on privacy benchmarks. These improvements, however, can come at the cost of task utility, due to the trade-off between reasoning performance and instruction-following abilities. Overall, our results show that improving instruction-following behavior in reasoning models can significantly enhance privacy, suggesting a promising direction for the development of future privacy-aware agents. Our code and data are available at https://github.com/UKPLab/arxiv2026-controllable-reasoning-models

AI.tldr: Training reasoning models to follow instructions in reasoning traces improves privacy preservation but trades off task utility.
AI.motivation: AI agents using reasoning models risk leaking sensitive user data through uncontrolled reasoning traces; improving instruction-following in reasoning could enhance privacy.
AI.method: Fine-tune models on instruction-following dataset with reasoning trace restrictions; use separate LoRA adapters to decouple reasoning and answer generation.
AI.result: Achieved up to 20.9-point improvement in instruction-following and 51.9 percentage-point gain on privacy benchmarks across 6 models (1.7B-14B parameters), though with task utility trade-offs.
AI.conclusion: Improving instruction-following in reasoning models significantly enhances privacy, offering a promising direction for privacy-aware AI agents despite utility trade-offs.

title: DARE-bench: Evaluating Modeling and Instruction Fidelity of LLMs in Data Science
comment: Published as a conference paper at ICLR 2026. 10 pages plus appendix
summary: The fast-growing demands in using Large Language Models (LLMs) to tackle complex multi-step data science tasks create an emergent need for accurate benchmarking. There are two major gaps in existing benchmarks: (i) the lack of standardized, process-aware evaluation that captures instruction adherence and process fidelity, and (ii) the scarcity of accurately labeled training data. To bridge these gaps, we introduce DARE-bench, a benchmark designed for machine learning modeling and data science instruction following. Unlike many existing benchmarks that rely on human- or model-based judges, all tasks in DARE-bench have verifiable ground truth, ensuring objective and reproducible evaluation. To cover a broad range of tasks and support agentic tools, DARE-bench consists of 6,300 Kaggle-derived tasks and provides both large-scale training data and evaluation sets. Extensive evaluations show that even highly capable models such as gpt-o4-mini struggle to achieve good performance, especially in machine learning modeling tasks. Using DARE-bench training tasks for fine-tuning can substantially improve model performance. For example, supervised fine-tuning boosts Qwen3-32B's accuracy by 1.83x and reinforcement learning boosts Qwen3-4B's accuracy by more than 8x. These significant improvements verify the importance of DARE-bench both as an accurate evaluation benchmark and critical training data.

AI.tldr: DARE-bench is a benchmark for evaluating LLMs on multi-step data science tasks with verifiable ground truth, addressing gaps in standardized process-aware evaluation and training data scarcity.
AI.motivation: Existing benchmarks lack standardized process-aware evaluation that captures instruction adherence and process fidelity, and suffer from scarcity of accurately labeled training data for complex multi-step data science tasks.
AI.method: Introduced DARE-bench with 6,300 Kaggle-derived tasks featuring verifiable ground truth (not relying on human/model judges). Provides both large-scale training data and evaluation sets covering broad range of tasks with support for agentic tools.
AI.result: Even highly capable models like gpt-o4-mini struggle, especially in ML modeling tasks. Fine-tuning with DARE-bench training data substantially improves performance: supervised fine-tuning boosts Qwen3-32B accuracy by 1.83x, reinforcement learning boosts Qwen3-4B accuracy by >8x.
AI.conclusion: DARE-bench serves as both an accurate evaluation benchmark and critical training data source, with significant performance improvements demonstrating its importance for advancing LLM capabilities in data science tasks.

title: Do LLMs Benefit From Their Own Words?
summary: Multi-turn interactions with large language models typically retain the assistant's own past responses in the conversation history. In this work, we revisit this design choice by asking whether large language models benefit from conditioning on their own prior responses. Using in-the-wild, multi-turn conversations, we compare standard (full-context) prompting with a user-turn-only prompting approach that omits all previous assistant responses, across three open reasoning models and one state-of-the-art model. To our surprise, we find that removing prior assistant responses does not affect response quality on a large fraction of turns. Omitting assistant-side history can reduce cumulative context lengths by up to 10x. To explain this result, we find that multi-turn conversations consist of a substantial proportion (36.4%) of self-contained prompts, and that many follow-up prompts provide sufficient instruction to be answered using only the current user turn and prior user turns. When analyzing cases where user-turn-only prompting substantially outperforms full context, we identify instances of context pollution, in which models over-condition on their previous responses, introducing errors, hallucinations, or stylistic artifacts that propagate across turns. Motivated by these findings, we design a context-filtering approach that selectively omits assistant-side context. Our findings suggest that selectively omitting assistant history can improve response quality while reducing memory consumption.

AI.tldr: Removing prior assistant responses from LLM conversation history often doesn't hurt quality while reducing context length up to 10x, revealing many prompts are self-contained and assistant history can cause context pollution.
AI.motivation: To challenge the standard design choice of including LLMs' own prior responses in conversation history and investigate whether models truly benefit from conditioning on their own past outputs in multi-turn interactions.
AI.method: Compared standard full-context prompting with user-turn-only prompting (omitting all previous assistant responses) across three open reasoning models and one state-of-the-art model using in-the-wild multi-turn conversations. Analyzed prompt self-containment, designed context-filtering approach for selective omission.
AI.result: Removing prior assistant responses doesn't affect quality on many turns (36.4% prompts are self-contained), reduces context length up to 10x. User-turn-only prompting sometimes outperforms full context due to context pollution where models over-condition on previous responses, causing error propagation.
AI.conclusion: Selectively omitting assistant history can improve response quality while reducing memory consumption, challenging the necessity of always including LLMs' own prior responses in conversation context.

title: QD-MAPPER: A Quality Diversity Framework to Automatically Evaluate Multi-Agent Path Finding Algorithms in Diverse Maps
summary: We use the Quality Diversity (QD) algorithm with Neural Cellular Automata (NCA) to automatically evaluate Multi-Agent Path Finding (MAPF) algorithms by generating diverse maps. Previously, researchers typically evaluate MAPF algorithms on a set of specific, human-designed maps at their initial stage of algorithm design. However, such fixed maps may not cover all scenarios, and algorithms may overfit to the small set of maps. To seek further improvements, systematic evaluations on a diverse suite of maps are needed. In this work, we propose Quality-Diversity Multi-Agent Path Finding Performance EvaluatoR (QD-MAPPER), a general framework that takes advantage of the QD algorithm to comprehensively understand the performance of MAPF algorithms by generating maps with patterns, be able to make fair comparisons between two MAPF algorithms, providing further information on the selection between two algorithms and on the design of the algorithms. Empirically, we employ this technique to evaluate and compare the behavior of different types of MAPF algorithms, including search-based, priority-based, rule-based, and learning-based algorithms. Through both single-algorithm experiments and comparisons between algorithms, researchers can identify patterns that each MAPF algorithm excels and detect disparities in runtime or success rates between different algorithms.

AI.tldr: QD-MAPPER uses Quality Diversity algorithms with Neural Cellular Automata to automatically generate diverse maps for comprehensive evaluation of Multi-Agent Path Finding algorithms, enabling fair comparisons and algorithm design insights.
AI.motivation: Current MAPF algorithm evaluation relies on limited human-designed maps, which may cause overfitting and fail to cover all scenarios. Systematic evaluation on diverse maps is needed for fair comparisons and algorithm improvement.
AI.method: Proposes QD-MAPPER framework combining Quality Diversity algorithms with Neural Cellular Automata to automatically generate diverse maps with patterns for comprehensive MAPF algorithm evaluation and comparison.
AI.result: Enables evaluation of various MAPF algorithm types (search-based, priority-based, rule-based, learning-based) through single-algorithm experiments and algorithm comparisons, identifying performance patterns and disparities in runtime/success rates.
AI.conclusion: QD-MAPPER provides a systematic framework for comprehensive MAPF algorithm evaluation, enabling fair comparisons, algorithm selection guidance, and design insights through automated generation of diverse test maps.
